name: Amortized Analysis
intent: Price an operation by its average cost over a whole sequence of operations, so a rare expensive step (a resize, a rehash, a rebuild) can be paid for by the many cheap ones, and know when that average hides a cost you cannot afford.
scenario: A service appends every incoming event to an in-memory buffer, a dynamic array that doubles when it is full. Over 100,000 appends it makes 131,071 element copies in total, about 1.31 per append, so the append is O(1) amortized. One append, though, copies 65,536 elements in a row, and on a latency-sensitive path that single append shows up as a spike in the slowest requests.
problem: Worst-case analysis says an append can cost O(n) because the array may need to be copied, so a loop of n appends looks like O(n²). That is true of the worst single append and false of the sequence: the expensive resizes are rare and get rarer as the array grows. Without a way to average over the sequence, you would reject a perfectly good data structure. With only the average, you would miss that one operation in a request path can still be slow.

howItWorks.title: Cost the sequence, not the operation
howItWorks.text: Amortized analysis bounds the total cost of any sequence of n operations and divides by n. It is a guarantee about the worst sequence, with no probability involved: whatever the order of operations, the total is at most this. Average-case analysis is different: it averages over random inputs and needs assumptions about the data. Amortized cost needs none.

howItWorks.title: Dynamic array: double when full
howItWorks.text: An array has a capacity. Appending to a full one allocates a new array and copies every element across. If the new capacity is twice the old, the copies cost 1 + 2 + 4 + ... up to n/2 or n, which sums to less than 2n for n appends. Divide by n: fewer than 2 copies per append, so appending is O(1) amortized, even though one append can cost O(n).

howItWorks.title: Growth must be a factor, not a constant
howItWorks.text: Growing by a fixed amount (+10 each time) copies the whole array every 10 appends, so n appends cost about n²/20 copies: O(n) per append amortized. A multiplicative factor (1.5x, 2x) keeps the resizes geometrically rarer. Real runtimes choose their own factors, commonly somewhere between about 1.125x and 2x. A smaller factor wastes less spare memory and copies more often, a larger one the opposite.

howItWorks.title: The same trick elsewhere
howItWorks.text: A hash table that doubles its buckets and rehashes every key when the load factor passes a limit spreads that rehashing to O(1) amortized per insert for the same reason (the insert itself is O(1) only in expectation, which is a separate assumption about the hash). A binary counter that flips many bits only occasionally, a queue built from two stacks, and the merges of a log-structured store all pay a large cost rarely and a small one often. In each case the large step is paid for by the many small ones before it.

howItWorks.title: Do not shrink too eagerly, and watch the worst operation
howItWorks.text: If the array halves as soon as it is half empty, a workload that alternates one removal and one append at that boundary resizes on every operation: each cycle copies about the whole array. Shrinking only when it is a quarter full leaves slack so the cost really does amortize. And where the worst single operation matters (a request, a frame, a real-time loop), amortized O(1) is the wrong promise: pre-size the array, resize in small pieces, or use a structure with a worst-case bound.

pros: Explains why dynamic arrays, hash tables and similar structures are fast in practice despite an O(n) worst step
A real guarantee about any sequence of operations, with no assumption about the input distribution
Guides the design: a multiplicative growth factor, and a shrink threshold below the growth threshold
Gives a model for other structures that rebuild occasionally: two-stack queues, counters, log-structured merges
cons: Says nothing about the cost of one operation: the unlucky call still pays the whole bill
The averaging only holds over a long enough sequence; a short burst that triggers one big resize is not averaged away
Gets confused with average-case analysis, which is about random inputs and is a different claim
Spare capacity left by growth is memory the program holds and does not use
whenToUse: Judging data structures that grow or rebuild themselves: arrays, hash tables, buffers
Throughput-oriented work, where total time over many operations is what counts
Explaining why a loop of n appends is O(n) in total and not O(n²)
whenNotToUse: Real-time and latency-sensitive paths where one slow operation breaks a deadline: look at the worst case per operation
Short sequences, where a single rare expensive step is not diluted by many cheap ones
Structures that are shared and locked while they resize, since every waiting caller feels the single spike
pitfalls: Reading amortized O(1) as every operation is O(1): the average is bounded, one append may copy the whole array
Ignoring latency spikes: the resize is a rare event that lands on a real request, and it shows up in the slowest requests (p99.9, p99.99) and not in the average
Growing by a constant (+10, +1000): total copies become quadratic, so the cost per append is O(n) amortized
Choosing the growth factor without thinking about memory: doubling can leave nearly half the array unused, and during the copy the old and new arrays exist at the same time
Shrinking when the array is half empty and growing when it is full: an application that hovers at that boundary resizes on almost every operation (thrashing)
Mixing up amortized and average-case: amortized is a worst-case guarantee on a sequence, average-case is an expectation over random inputs
Forgetting that other costs are not amortized away: a resize while holding a lock stalls every other thread, and an allocation can be slow or fail
Not pre-sizing when n is known: reserving capacity up front removes the resizes entirely

quiz.question: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. After 1,000 appends, roughly how many element copies have resizes made in total?
options: About 500,000, because each append may copy the whole array.
About 10, one per doubling, since a resize is a single operation.
About 1,000,000, because each of 1,000 appends copies 1,000 elements.
About 1,000 (1,023 in the model), fewer than 2 per append.
quiz.explanation: Resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ... 512, and copy that many elements each: 1 + 2 + ... + 512 = 1,023. The total stays below 2n, which is why appending is O(1) amortized.

quiz.question: A growth policy adds a fixed 10 slots whenever the array is full. What does that do to the cost of n appends?
options: Total copies become about n²/20, so appending is O(n) amortized.
Nothing changes, since 10 slots at a time is still O(1) per append.
It is cheaper than doubling, because each resize copies fewer elements.
It is fine until n reaches 10,000, then it becomes constant again.
quiz.explanation: Resizes happen every 10 appends and each copies the whole array, so the total grows with the square of n (about 500 million copies at 100,000 appends, 5,000 per append). A multiplicative factor keeps resizes geometrically rarer.

quiz.question: An API appends to a doubling array under a latency budget, and the slowest 0.02% of requests are far slower than the rest. What is the most likely explanation and fix?
options: Amortized O(1) is wrong for arrays, so replace the array with a hash table.
The average cost is too high, so a smaller growth factor will lower it.
A resize copies the whole array in one append, so pre-size it or use a structure with a worst-case bound.
The allocator is faulty, because every append should cost the same.
quiz.explanation: Amortized O(1) bounds the average over a sequence, not one append. The rare append that triggers a resize pays for all the elements, and that is the spike. Reserving capacity up front, or growing incrementally, removes it.
